cases.title: Orissa State Roads Project: 1,376 land awards unpaid and 1,890 people ruled out of resettlement
cases.place: Bhawanipatna-Khariar, Anandapur-Bhadrak-Chandbali, Berhampur-Taptapani and Jagatpur-Chandbali roads, Odisha, India
cases.point: Bhawanipatna, Kalahandi district, at the start of the 68 km Bhawanipatna-Khariar road (NH-16), the first of four road packages. The project ran about 310 km of road through 263 villages in Odisha, so one point cannot cover it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-75770 for the Orissa State Roads Project (P096023). US$250 million approved 30 September 2008, effective 15 April 2009, closing moved from 31 December 2014 to 30 June 2016. The loan was cut to US$163 million, US$87 million was cancelled and US$79.28 million was disbursed. Total project cost US$134.22 million against US$322.50 million planned, with the Government of Odisha paying US$54.94 million (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 17 February 2017).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A. Three social safeguard policies were triggered at preparation: indigenous peoples (OP/BP 4.10), physical cultural resources (OP/BP 4.11) and involuntary resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). The completion report says the indigenous peoples policy was in fact not triggered during implementation, because the roads finally chosen left out the roads in tribal areas. The resettlement policy the project adopted made squatter tenants ineligible for resettlement assistance, and also made squatters who were only partly affected ineligible. Land was taken under the Land Acquisition Act 1894 as amended in 1984 up to 31 December 2013, and under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 from 1 January 2014 (World Bank completion report, Annex 9, Summary of Social Safeguards Activities).

companies.name: SMEC
companies.role: First construction supervision consultant on the project. The Government of Odisha's own section of the completion report says its services were terminated in August 2010 'due to misrepresented facts'. The report gives no further detail and the company's answer is not in it.

cases.community: The figures below are from Annex 9 of the Bank's completion report, its summary of social safeguards activities. 7,948 project-affected people were enumerated along the four road corridors. Of those, 1,890 were ruled ineligible for resettlement help, because some were outside the alignment after it was marked out and because the project's own resettlement policy excluded squatter tenants and partly affected squatters. The report gives two different numbers for how many were eligible, 6,050 in one paragraph and 6,058 in the next, and does not explain the gap. 5,730 of the eligible people had been relocated and 328 had not. Of 828 people who lost a home, 730 were relocated and 632 had rebuilt a house. Of 3,130 whose shop or other commercial structure was hit, 2,915 were relocated and 2,700 had rebuilt. Of 2,100 who lost a kiosk, 2,070 were relocated and 2,085 had rebuilt. On compensation for land, 7,698 cases or awards were made and the owners in 6,312 of them had been paid INR 604,582,870; INR 110,740,687 was still owed on 1,376 cases. Of those 1,376, 253 could not be paid because the owners had gone to court, mostly asking for more money, and 84 were held up at the Endowment Commissioner over disputed temple land. A further INR 4,080,642 was paid into civil deposits with the courts because owners had not come to collect it; the report lists missing inheritance papers, unwillingness to share the money and the cost of travelling to collect sums the owners thought too small among the reasons, and says the project treats payment into civil deposits as as good as paying the compensation. On resettlement assistance to farmers who lost land, 4,258 of 4,995 eligible people were paid in year one and 1,235 of 2,288 in year two, with 492 of the rest paid into court deposits and 561 still in progress when the report was written. The project's complaint handling system received 626 complaints between 9 October 2009 and 15 August 2016, of which 495 had been resolved, 66 were at hearing and 65 were pending; the report says they were about compensation payments, rehabilitation assistance, people seeking to be added to the affected list, and the nature and use of structures to be moved. Fifteen petitions were made under India's right to information law.
cases.suppression: No arrests, forced evictions or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. Complaints of corruption on the project were passed to the Bank's Integrity Vice Presidency, which the completion report says was still investigating.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.displaced_note: 5,730 eligible project-affected people had been relocated, out of 7,948 enumerated, per the World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report of 17 February 2017. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 64,287, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014. The Bank's report does not say how many of the 7,948 lost a home rather than part of a plot or a roadside pitch beyond the 828 it counts as losing a residential structure.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and the borrower's performance Unsatisfactory. For more than nine months in the first year, road contractors could not take possession of sites because land acquisition and compensation payment were not finished. The Bank suspended loan disbursements and set out eight actions the state had to meet before the suspension could be lifted; the report says it took 17 months, from May 2011 to October 2012, before the state substantially complied. 150 km of road were improved by closing, against a revised target of 303 km and an original target of 461 km. The project's public-private partnership support part was removed from the project because of noncompliance by the Government of Odisha with the Bank's safeguard policies. The remaining resettlement was carried into construction the state paid for itself after the loan closed. A study of social safeguards and social development impacts was commissioned from the Nabakrishna Choudhury Centre for Development Studies in Bhubaneswar and was not finished when the completion report was written.

sources.title: India - Orissa State Roads Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR00003903)
ICR Review: India - IN: Orissa State Roads (P096023)
Evicted and Abandoned: India Orissa State Roads Project (P096023)

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on the Bank's own documents alone: its completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report, which is the Bank's own evaluators reading the same report. The lender is reporting on its own project. The two documents give the same unpaid-award count, 1,376, and the same relocation count, 5,730. The completion report's own numbers for eligible people do not agree with each other, 6,050 and 6,058, and both are printed here. The relocation and payment figures in Annex 9 are the project unit's own monitoring data. No press report, court record or NGO field research on this project was found, and the study of what happened to the resettled people was unfinished at the time of the report.
cases.ecosystem: Trees were felled along the corridors. The completion report says there were substantial deficiencies in carrying out environmental management safeguards, particularly on regulatory compliance, work site management, traffic management during construction and the management of construction camps, and that supervision consultants and contractors paid too little attention to the environmental management plans, which were corrected after the Bank intervened. The report's stakeholder workshop annex records that the Odisha Forest Development Corporation planted 176,000 saplings as compensatory planting.

lvwhy.project: An IBRD road loan paid for the works that took the land.
lvwhy.land: Private titled land was acquired across 263 villages and roadside occupiers were cleared from the right of way.

cases.title: Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement: compensation paid into court, tax taken off payments
cases.place: Karnataka state highways, including Malavalli-Pavagada, Mudhol-Nippani, Anandhapura-Shikaripura and Managili-Devapura, India
cases.point: Hungsagi village, Yadgiri district, where 27 resettled families still had no ownership title to their plots in June 2019. The project covered road works in several parts of Karnataka, so one point cannot cover it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-80220 for the Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement Project (P107649). US$350 million approved 24 March 2011, cut to US$295.2 million, all of which was disbursed. Closing was moved from 31 December 2016 to 28 December 2018. The completion report also lists trust fund TF-92428 (US$0.44 million original, US$0.18 million disbursed) and gives the project's effectiveness date as 17 July 2008 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 October 2019).

lenders.name: Foreign private commercial sources (unidentified)
lenders.role: The Bank's completion report's financing table lists US$500 million at approval from 'Foreign Private Commercial Sources (unidentified)', revised to US$400 million, with US$416 million actually provided. The report does not name the lenders. The same report records US$416.56 million as the amount of new private sector capital the Government of Karnataka generated for improving and managing the state's core road network, which was one of the project's own outcome targets.

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered OP/BP 4.12 on involuntary resettlement and OP/BP 4.11 on physical cultural resources. A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared and the policy was changed in 2014 to fit India's new land acquisition law. The project paid an extra 25 per cent compensation to landowners who agreed to the rates offered.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report records 602 acres of private land taken from about 6,800 landowners, about 2,200 informal occupiers affected, and about 200 households physically displaced, of whom about 140 were informal occupiers. The independent evaluation the project commissioned at midterm in 2014 found living standards had risen on average, and also found that more than 90 per cent of affected people were not satisfied with the compensation amounts and that about 20 per cent had gone to court to get the amounts raised. The end-term evaluation in 2019, based on a survey of 700 affected families and a comparison group of 110 households, found a large proportion of compensation money, especially on the state highways side, had been paid into the courts because owners lacked ownership documents, and that 'these people faced several hardships in realizing the compensation amounts from the courts with high legal fees, long delays, multiple court hearings'. The same study found income tax had been deducted from compensation paid to people losing houses and structures in residential areas, which it says is against the resettlement policy adopted for the project; it names 7 landowners whose deductions were made by the state highways unit and 67 by the Karnataka Road Development Corporation, which the report says have to be repaid under the policy applied to the project. The completion report says over 40 per cent of compensation amounts were deposited with the courts, that the grievance committees were not functioning and that the database for tracking land acquisition and resettlement was not functioning. 1,235 complaints were made to the state highways unit and 543 to the road development corporation. In the 2019 survey about 15 per cent of affected people on the state highways side said their incomes were lower after resettlement, 52 per cent said they were the same and about a third said they had improved.
cases.suppression: No arrests or police action are recorded. The completion report records 24 acres the corporation could not take possession of because landowners resisted until the courts released their compensation.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.displaced_note: About 200 households physically displaced, about 140 of them informal occupiers, with about 6,800 landowners losing land and about 2,200 informal occupiers affected, per the World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report of 23 October 2019. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 15,516, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014.
cases.displaced_label: households physically displaced (World Bank completion report)
cases.outcome: The Bank's rating for compliance with its resettlement policy, OP 4.12, stayed Unsatisfactory or Moderately Unsatisfactory for over three years, and the Bank and the state agreed remedial plans to bring the project back into compliance. The Independent Evaluation Group says 93 per cent of the land acquisition activities had been completed when the loan closed in December 2018. Outstanding in June 2019: compensation to 21 landowners not yet announced, resettlement assistance to 6 families, ownership titles for 27 families at the Hungsagi resettlement site in Yadgiri district, the resettlement of 31 displaced of Thangadagi village in Bijapur district, which the report does not say are people or families, 24 acres the corporation could not take possession of, and 6.23 acres of new land acquisition in 15 villages for drain improvements. The Bank rated the project's overall outcome Satisfactory and its own performance Satisfactory.

sources.title: India - Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
ICR Review: India - IN: Karnataka State Highway Improv Pro II (P107649)
Evicted and Abandoned: Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement (P107649)

cases.confidence_note: The core harm rests on the Bank's own documents alone: its completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The lender is reporting on its own project. The findings on compensation paid into court, on income tax deducted against the project's own resettlement policy, and on the two named villages are in the completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group repeats them. The dissatisfaction and income figures come from two impact evaluations the project itself commissioned from consultants, in 2014 and 2019, not from independent field research. The same documents record rises in housing quality and asset ownership among resettled households, and both sets of findings are given here. No press report, court record or NGO field research on this project was found.
cases.ecosystem: Trees were felled along the corridors. The completion report says 153,000 saplings were planted in compensatory planting against a plan of over 223,000, with the remaining 73,500 due by December 2019, and gives too few saplings, the rains and delays in finishing road stretches as the reasons. The project closed with a Satisfactory rating on environmental safeguard management.

lvwhy.project: An IBRD loan paid for widening the state highways that took the land.
lvwhy.land: 602 acres of private land were acquired and about 2,200 informal occupiers were moved off the right of way.

cases.title: Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project: landslides, debris, and land occupied beyond what was acquired
cases.place: Himachal Pradesh core road network, India
cases.point: Shimla, the state capital and seat of the Himachal Pradesh Road and Other Infrastructure Development Corporation, which ran the project. The works were spread over about 355 km of upgraded road and 1,831 km of maintained road across the state, so one point cannot cover it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loans IBRD-48600 (US$220 million approved 5 June 2007, US$219,998,008 disbursed) and IBRD-81990, an additional loan of US$61.7 million cut to US$46.7 million, all disbursed, for the Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project (P096019). Effective 5 October 2007; closing moved from 30 June 2013 to 30 June 2017. The state paid US$98.51 million of the US$365.21 million total (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 December 2017).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered five safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement and forests. Resettlement action plans were prepared for each road package and an NGO was engaged to help carry them out. The additional loan's project agreement added a covenant on the implementing corporation.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says land acquisition and resettlement 'often was slow', and gives the reasons as poor coordination between the implementing corporation and the Land Acquisition Officer, inaccurate information about land holdings in the resettlement action plans, mismatches between road design drawings and revenue maps, changes of alignment, and delays in negotiations and payments. In a footnote the report records that the Bank rated social safeguards performance Moderately Unsatisfactory at two consecutive supervision missions in 2008 and 2009, because the post of social development officer in the implementing corporation was vacant, no NGO was in place to deliver resettlement and rehabilitation assistance, and the corporation failed to act on allegations that contractors had occupied private land in excess of what had been acquired. The report says those problems were eventually remedied. Of the total compensation due, 96.2 per cent had been paid when the loan closed on 30 June 2017. The report says the amounts left unpaid on packages 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 were for reasons outside the corporation's control: owners had died with heirs not yet on record, there were court cases or stays, and co-owners were in dispute. Of the total resettlement and rehabilitation assistance due, 93.5 per cent had been paid; the report gives the reasons for the rest as owners not coming to collect despite notices, court cases, and people who could not be traced. The report gives no number of project-affected people anywhere. About 12 km of road were cut from several packages because of land acquisition problems. A survey of affected people on the ten upgrading packages in October, November and December 2016 found women recipients reporting nearly 100 per cent positive answers on better access to work, public services, safety and markets.
cases.suppression: No arrests, forced evictions or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report, which does record workplace safety among the problems on four contracts.
cases.displaced_note: No count of displaced people appears in the World Bank completion report; the results framework sets a land acquisition target of 132 hectares and 154 hectares of forest land diverted. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 16,896, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014. There is no Bank figure here to set against ICIJ's.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Satisfactory. 355 km of the state core road network were upgraded from single to two lanes, against a target of 447 km. Environmental performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for several months from late 2014 over what the Independent Evaluation Group calls 'serious problems' on contracts 5-I, 5-II, 6-I and 6-II: poor debris management, protection of forest lands, dust pollution, road safety and workplace safety. The completion report records that in September 2011 poor planning and sequencing of works on contract 9 caused several large landslides that blocked access for vehicles and people, and that an unprecedented landslide later delayed the same contract, forcing the contractor to remove debris and repair damaged pavement. About 80 debris disposal sites were later rehabilitated using bioengineering, and 432,692 trees were planted with a 69.75 per cent survival rate.

sources.title: India - Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
ICR Review: India - IN: HP State Roads Project (P096019)
Evicted and Abandoned: Himachal Pradesh State Roads Project (P096019)

cases.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The lender is reporting on its own project. No named community, court record, press report or NGO field research on this project was found. The completion report gives no count of affected people, read in full from the 56-page report, so the scale of the land taking cannot be checked against ICIJ's estimate. The documented harm here is environmental and procedural: the Bank's own Moderately Unsatisfactory environmental rating over debris management and forest protection, landslides caused by poor sequencing of works, and the 2008-2009 finding that the implementing corporation did not act on allegations that contractors had taken more private land than was acquired. The unpaid residuals of 3.8 per cent of compensation and 6.5 per cent of resettlement assistance are small shares of the total and the Bank attributes them to deaths, court cases and untraceable owners rather than to the project; they are not presented here as a compensation failure.
cases.ecosystem: 154 hectares of forest land were diverted for the roads. Environmental performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for months over poor debris management and failure to protect forest lands on four contracts, and poor sequencing of works caused landslides on one contract in September 2011. Himachal Pradesh is a steep Himalayan state where the construction season is about six months a year.

lvwhy.project: Two IBRD loans paid for the road upgrading and maintenance works.
lvwhy.land: Land was acquired along the upgraded roads and 154 hectares of forest land were diverted.

cases.title: Lucknow-Muzaffarpur National Highway: 442 hectares taken from 23,394 landholders
cases.place: NH-28 between Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh and Muzaffarpur, Bihar, India
cases.point: Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, about midway along the NH-28 corridor the project widened. The corridor runs across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, so one point cannot cover it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-47640 for the Lucknow-Muzaffarpur National Highway Project (P077856). US$620 million approved 21 December 2004, effective 28 December 2005, closing moved from 30 June 2010 to 30 June 2012, US$615.70 million disbursed. Implemented by the National Highways Authority of India (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 December 2012).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A. Entitlements were to be delivered under a resettlement action plan for each phase, under the Bank's resettlement policy of the time, operational directive 3.40. The Bank agreed to keep monitoring resettlement on corridor sections it did not finance until they were finished, under the project's resettlement policy and the project agreement.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report describes the project's displacement and resettlement impacts as 'high in magnitude as well as intensity' and counts the taking of 442 hectares of private land from about 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title, and 259 religious properties. It says that by the closing date land acquisition and resettlement were fully completed and all affected families had received their compensation and main entitlements, except a few whose cases were in court over who owned the land. Four religious properties could not be moved because religious leaders took hard positions. Stretches of land totalling up to 1,800 metres were taken out of the project because ownership disputes took too long to settle; the highways authority said it would do that work with its own money. Over the life of the project the Bank's own ratings for resettlement implementation moved from satisfactory to unsatisfactory and back to satisfactory. The consultants who were to evaluate what happened to resettled people at the end of the project were not hired until the closing date, so that evaluation was still under way; the Independent Evaluation Group says the Bank would keep monitoring it until the final report was submitted. The Independent Evaluation Group notes that the completion report does not state that all safeguards were met or complied with. At stakeholder workshops the general view reported was that land acquisition and resettlement 'was done reasonably well except for a few stray cases of dissatisfaction', and that landowners along the road were pleased because their asset values had risen; many people at the same workshops said road safety had worsened because of higher speeds.
cases.suppression: No arrests, forced evictions or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.displaced_note: 442 hectares of private land taken from about 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title, per the World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report of 13 December 2012; 23,394 is the sum of the report's two figures. The report does not say how many people lost a home as against part of a field or a roadside pitch. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 75,434, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014.
cases.displaced_label: titled and untitled holders of land taken (sum of the World Bank completion report's two figures)
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory. Land acquisition, tree cutting and utility shifting delayed the works and the project was restructured in May 2010 and June 2012, with contracts 9 to 12 taken out of it. Environmental compliance in the early years is described as patchy and moved from satisfactory to unsatisfactory before returning to satisfactory. At the time of the report the Bank was still monitoring clean-up work in some sections and camps, drainage issues on contracts 1 to 3, and drainage, slope protection and debris clearance on the Gorakhpur bypass, which the Bank did not fund but monitored as a linked project. The end-of-project study of what happened to resettled people had not been completed when the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review were written.

sources.title: India - Lucknow-Muzaffarpur National Highway Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
ICR Review: India - Lucknow Muzaffarpur National Highway Project (P077856)
Evicted and Abandoned: Lucknow-Muzaffarpur National Highway Project (P077856)

cases.confidence_note: This is a large land taking that the Bank's own documents record as finished with compensation paid, not a record of a failure. The gaps in the record are that the Bank's rating for resettlement implementation fell to unsatisfactory at points during the project, that the consultants who were to assess what happened to resettled people were not hired until the closing date so that no completed assessment exists, and that the Independent Evaluation Group states the completion report does not say safeguards were met and complied with. An unmeasured outcome is not a measured harm, and none is claimed here. No press report, court record or NGO field research on this corridor's resettlement was found, and the only account of how affected people felt is the stakeholder workshop summary inside the Bank's own report. The lender is reporting on its own project.
cases.ecosystem: Trees were cut along the corridor and compensatory planting was carried out. The completion report records drainage problems on contracts 1 to 3 and drainage, slope protection and debris clearance problems on the Gorakhpur bypass still open at closing, and says borrow areas were rehabilitated as farmland and ponds.

lvwhy.project: An IBRD loan of US$620 million paid for four-laning NH-28.
lvwhy.land: 442 hectares of private land were taken from about 23,394 titled and untitled holders.

cases.title: Mizan-Dima road and the Biftu quarry: dust, blasting damage, seven deaths and a suspended World Bank credit
cases.place: Mizan-Dima road contract and the Biftu quarry that supplied it, south-west Ethiopia
cases.point: Mizan Teferi, at the eastern end of the Mizan-Dima road contract. The Bank's documents do not give coordinates for the Biftu quarry or for the village beside it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-51550 for the Ethiopia Transport Sector Project in Support of RSDP4 (P117731). US$415 million approved 25 September 2012, effective 25 January 2013, cut to US$290.9 million, US$262.7 million disbursed, closed 26 October 2018 instead of 30 April 2019. The Ethiopian Roads Authority was the implementing agency. The Bank partially suspended disbursement on the Mizan-Dima contract in January 2018 and the suspension ran until the credit closed (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 September 2019).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A. Environmental and social impact assessments, resettlement action plans and environmental and social management plans were required for each civil works site, and the management plans included measures to limit dust near villages at the quarry. Contractors were required to prepare site-specific plans. The Bank's partial suspension of disbursement was lifted only on completion of an agreed action plan.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report records complaints from the village beside the Biftu quarry, which supplied stone for the Mizan-Dima road, between November 2015 and April 2016, about resettlement compensation values, excessive dust from the crusher plant, drainage, and damage to property. It says the problems at the quarry should have been dealt with by moving people and controlling dust to a high standard, 'but it was not fully managed at site', and that the contractor failed to carry out measures the supervising consultant asked for. The Ethiopian Roads Authority's own comments, printed in the same report, say the complaint came from one local resident and farm owner, that two independent experts reported in December 2016 that the affected area should be 150 metres from the centre of the crusher and blasting site and that compensation should be paid to everyone inside it, and that the experts found 'there is no any damage that occur on the initial complaint'. The roads authority's list of what it then paid is its own account: compensation to more than 4,000 affected people for disturbance from the contractor's operations, more than 15 million Birr for lost crop production inside the agreed area, compensation to 372 households for damage from the contractor's blasting, monthly payments to 25 vulnerable groups, and 20 corporate groups set up to run their own businesses. It says more than 95 per cent of complaints were compensated. The Bank's own text says more than 95 per cent of complainants obtained appropriate compensation for the damage that occurred, but that the action plan was not fully completed. The roads authority's comments also say the quarry at kilometre 39, the Biftu quarry, was used on the supervising consultant's recommendation because a security problem near the only other suitable stone source, at kilometre 80.5, made that site hard to reach.
cases.suppression: No arrests, evictions by force or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report. The roads authority's comments in the same report dispute the Bank's account of its handling of the complaints and say the suspension was imposed before the action plan was agreed.
cases.killed_note: The Bank's completion report says in a footnote that 19 fatal accidents occurred in the project: 2 on Kombolcha-Mille, 4 on Konso-Yabello, 7 on Mizan-Dima and 6 on Ambo-Woliso, during the construction periods. The 7 counted here are the Mizan-Dima figure. The other 12 were on three other road contracts under the same credit and are not counted on this card. The report sets the deaths under problems with occupational health and safety on the contracts, and records that the Bank raised the high level of fatalities at construction sites when the project was appraised. It does not say who the people were, how each died, or whether any of the 7 died at the Biftu quarry. Compensation to the families of the victims of fatal accidents was among the actions the Bank still required after the credit closed.
cases.displaced_note: The Bank's completion report gives no count of people displaced by the project. The Ethiopian Roads Authority's own comments in the report say more than 4,000 affected people were compensated for disturbance from the contractor's operations at the quarry and 372 households for blasting damage; these are the borrower's figures and count payments, not displacement. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 16,902, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's environmental and social management Unsatisfactory, its own performance Unsatisfactory and the overall outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory. It issued notices on the quarry problems, cleared an action plan the roads authority prepared in February 2017, and suspended disbursement on the Mizan-Dima contract in January 2018 when that plan's implementation became unsatisfactory; the suspension ran to the credit's closing in October 2018. The Mizan-Dima contract was finished in April 2019, after closing. A few actions under the quarry action plan were still outstanding when the completion report was written in September 2019. A health and safety action plan was agreed after the fatal accidents, and the roads authority's safeguards staff were increased and moved to directorate level at the end of 2018. The report also records security problems, which it describes as social unrest, at the Mizan-Dima sites through the works period, and major delays in moving electric poles early in the contract.

sources.title: Ethiopia - Transport Sector Project in Support of RSDP4: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Evicted and Abandoned: Ethiopia-Transport Sector Project in Support of RSDP4 (P117731)

cases.confidence_note: The Bank's completion report is the only source found for this episode, and the borrower's comments inside the same report contradict the Bank's account. The Bank says the contractor failed to carry out the measures asked for and that dust and blasting caused damage; the Ethiopian Roads Authority says independent experts found no damage from the original complaint and that the Bank suspended disbursement before an action plan had been agreed. The payment figures are the roads authority's own. No independent press report or NGO field research on the Biftu quarry was found.
cases.ecosystem: A crusher plant and blasting site at the Biftu quarry put dust over nearby farmland and homes and the Bank's documents record drainage problems and crop production loss in the surrounding fields. The roads authority had experts from Jimma Agricultural Institute assess agricultural production loss from the crushing work.

lvwhy.project: An IDA credit paid for the Mizan-Dima road contract and the quarry that supplied it.
lvwhy.land: Compensation was paid for land and crops inside a 150-metre affected area set around the crusher and blasting site.

cases.title: Mekenajo-Dembidolo road: flooding and lost coffee trees on an Ethiopian road loan
cases.place: Mekenajo-Dembidolo road corridor, western Oromia, Ethiopia
cases.point: Dambidollo (Dembidolo), Kelem Wellega zone, Oromia, at one end of the Mekenajo-Dembidolo road corridor. The Bank's documents do not give coordinates for the sections where flooding was reported.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-45610 (Credit 4561-ET) for the Road Sector Development Program Support Project IV, an adaptable programme loan (P106872). US$245 million approved 2 June 2009, effective 14 September 2009, revised to US$204.92 million, with US$206.28 million disbursed. Closing was extended from 30 June 2016 to 30 June 2017. The Government of Ethiopia cancelled SDR 24.12 million, about US$33 million, of the unwithdrawn credit on 7 April 2017. The borrower's contribution is recorded as zero against an appraisal estimate of US$63.2 million, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives no reason for that. The completion report's cost figures do not agree with each other: its data sheet gives a total project cost of US$206.3 million and its Table 7.6 gives US$275.2 million, which the Independent Evaluation Group records as incorrect or confusing (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 May 2018; World Bank Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, 6 November 2018).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. Contractors were required to prepare site-specific environmental management plans within 28 days of starting work. Slope protection by grassing was to be rooted before contractors left site.
cases.community: The project upgraded three road corridors, among them the 181 km Mekenajo-Dembidolo road in western Oromia. The Bank's completion report says the project assessed project-affected people before construction began and that the Ethiopian Roads Authority 'ensured that all PAPs were compensated' following the environmental and social impact assessment. Annex 10 of the same report, a summary of the Transport and Poverty Observatory study carried out on four of the programme's corridors from 2012 to 2016 using household surveys, focus group discussions and interviews, says instead that 'complaints regarding compensation were raised in all road corridors', and that the size of land lost to the road construction, the number of affected people compensated for the loss of their produce and the amounts paid were still being worked out by the roads authority when the report was written. Both statements are printed here and neither explains the other. On the Mekenajo-Dembidolo corridor the same annex says 'the problem of flooding has been widely observed in the Mekenajo-Dembidolo road corridor, where several coffee-growing farmers reported losing coffee trees and other perennial crops'. It also says that in some places dust was strong enough to affect traffic movement and cause vehicle accidents while construction was going on. The report says the roads authority pays compensation but the Regional Rural Authority and the woreda administrations provide land for relocation, that the woredas had little knowledge of safeguard compliance despite having the safeguard documents in the local language, and that the provision of land was slow; more than 90 per cent of affected people had been relocated by closing and the rest shortly after. Site-specific environmental management plans started more than 10 months after construction began, against the 28 days the contracts required. On the same corridor the report records that trees and grass planted to hold cut slopes had not taken root in many places even well after the road was handed over. The Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report does not report the number of people relocated and does not include a statement on whether the project complied with the safeguard policies.
cases.suppression: No arrests, evictions by force or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it.
cases.displaced_note: No count of displaced or relocated people appears in the World Bank completion report. The report records only that more than 90 per cent of affected people had been relocated by closing, and the Independent Evaluation Group states that the report does not give the number of people relocated. The report also says the size of land lost and the number of people compensated were still being worked out by the Ethiopian Roads Authority when it was written. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 27,401, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014. There is no Bank outcome figure here to set against ICIJ's.
cases.outcome: The 89 km Ankober-Dulecha-Awash Arba road was dropped from the project during restructuring in 2015 because of procurement and implementation delays and was later paid for with local funds. The Independent Evaluation Group says the implementation of safeguards was not effective because contractors were unable to carry out the environmental and social management plan, and that the completion report gave insufficient detail on safeguards for a category A project with resettlement. The mid-term review had already noted deficiencies in carrying out the management plan and the resettlement action plan. The report records that the roads authority recovered from the delay in environmental plans by carrying out mitigation measures that were paid items in the bill of quantities, including replacement tree planting and grassing of cut slopes.

cases.confidence_note: The harm rests on the Bank's own documents. The flooding and the lost coffee trees are in Annex 10 of the Bank's completion report, which summarises the Transport and Poverty Observatory study of four of the programme's corridors; the losses are what coffee farmers reported to that study, not a finding by anyone who inspected the fields. The completion report's main text says all affected people were compensated, while its own annex says complaints about compensation were raised on every corridor and that the roads authority had not yet worked out how much land was lost or how many people were paid. No press report, court record or NGO field research on this corridor was found, and the lender is reporting on its own project.
cases.ecosystem: The completion report's Annex 10 says flooding was widely observed along the Mekenajo-Dembidolo corridor and that coffee-growing farmers reported losing coffee trees and other perennial crops. Grass and trees planted to hold cut slopes had not rooted in many places well after the road was handed over, which the report says leaves the slopes unprotected. The project was environmental category A and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement.

lvwhy.project: An IDA adaptable programme loan paid for the road works.
lvwhy.land: Land was taken along the corridors and replacement land for affected people was slow to come.

cases.title: Caldwell Bridge and the Monrovia-Buchanan road: compensation late, and five cheques stolen
cases.place: Caldwell Bridge, Monrovia, and the Cotton Tree-Bokay Town-Buchanan road, Liberia
cases.point: Caldwell, Monrovia, at the new Caldwell Bridge, which links Caldwell to Bushrod Island and downtown Monrovia. The project also covered the Cotton Tree-Bokay Town-Buchanan road and streets in Monrovia, so one point cannot cover it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban and Rural Infrastructure Rehabilitation Project (P113099), approved 21 April 2009, effective 21 July 2009, closing moved from 30 June 2014 to 30 June 2017. IDA grants and credits IDA-H4780 (US$44 million), IDA-H6040 (US$20 million) and IDA-53510 (US$19.6 million). Under the project's second additional financing the Bank allocated US$8.0 million of IDA funds to pay resettlement action plan compensation under this project and under the Road Asset Management Project, because the government could not fund it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 December 2017).

lenders.name: Liberia Reconstruction Trust Fund (World Bank-administered)
lenders.role: Trust funds TF-94353 (US$9.2 million), TF-98040 (US$27 million original, US$25.2 million disbursed) and TF-16065 (US$9.4 million original, US$8.4 million disbursed). The fund was set up in 2007 by the European Union and other partners, which the completion report lists as Germany, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Britain and the Bank's Low Income Country Under Stress trust fund. Total project financing was US$126.9 million, with no borrower contribution.

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B. The only social safeguard policy triggered was involuntary resettlement, OP/BP 4.12, under which the government was to compensate affected people before sites were cleared and handed to contractors. Resettlement action plans governed the Caldwell Bridge, the Cotton Tree-Buchanan road and the Monrovia-Buchanan road.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says carrying out the resettlement action plans was hurt by the government not having enough money to compensate affected people, especially on the Cotton Tree-Buchanan road and the Caldwell Bridge, and that the government was caught out when civil works moved faster than expected and needed large sums to clear the right of way. On the Caldwell Bridge works, late payment of affected people delayed handing the site to the contractor, and the government paid the contractor US$315,000 in compensation as a result. The report records frequent delays in the actual payment of money to affected people, caused by poor coordination between the government bodies involved. On the Monrovia-Buchanan road it says carrying out the resettlement plan was held back by inadequate information being given out, by there being no community-level grievance mechanism, and by disagreements over how compensation was assessed. In 2016, five compensation cheques totalling US$11,348 were stolen from the office of the Project Financial Management Unit in the Ministry of Finance and illegally cashed; the government refunded the stolen funds to the Bank and the unit installed cameras to watch the movements of staff and clients. The report does not record whether the five people whose cheques were stolen were paid again.
cases.suppression: No arrests, evictions by force or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review. The Bank's report says its decision to fund the resettlement payments 'may have pre-empted significant local tension and conflict risks in the project area'.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
cases.displaced_note: The Bank's completion report gives no count of affected or displaced people for this project. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 18,770, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014. There is no Bank figure here to set against ICIJ's.
cases.outcome: The new Caldwell Bridge and its approaches, 670 metres in all, were built, linking Caldwell to Bushrod Island and downtown Monrovia. The Bank says that with the benefit of hindsight its decision to put US$8.0 million of IDA money into resettlement payments was right, because defaults in paying affected people threatened to delay the works badly and would have left the government facing contractors' claims. The report says all resettlement issues were addressed and documented by the end of the project. The Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives little detail on safeguards compliance and financial management.

cases.confidence_note: The late payments, the US$315,000 paid to the contractor and the five stolen cheques are all recorded in the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report is the only other source found. The lender is reporting on its own project. No count of affected people, no named community and no press report or NGO field research on this project's resettlement were found, so the scale cannot be checked against ICIJ's estimate.
cases.ecosystem: The project was rated environmental category B, partial assessment. The Bank's documents record no finding of damage to land or water.

lvwhy.project: IDA grants and a World Bank-administered trust fund paid for the bridge and roads, and IDA money later paid the resettlement compensation itself.
lvwhy.land: The right of way for the bridge approaches and the roads was cleared of occupiers, who had to be compensated before the sites were handed over.

extend.why: ICIJ lead 31 is the Lagos Metropolitan Development and Governance Project, P071340, credit IDA-42190, which the existing case already names as IDA Credit 4219 UNI with the same approval date of 6 July 2006 and the same closing date of 30 September 2013. It is the same credit and the same episode, so this is an extension rather than a new case. The additions come from the project's Implementation Completion and Results Report of 15 October 2013, which the existing card does not cite and which answers the card's statement that no results figures for the project were found.

additions.lenders_role_detail: The completion report gives the credit as IDA-42190, with an original commitment of XDR 138.10 million, of which XDR 90.11 million was disbursed. Approved 6 July 2006, effective 16 February 2007, restructured 5 July 2011, closed 30 September 2013 as originally planned. The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and the borrower's Moderately Unsatisfactory. The project was rated environmental category B.
additions.community_additions: The completion report records a social safeguards audit the Bank ordered. Its findings were a lack of clarity among those involved about what the safeguard policies were for; weak documentation, with community and asset mapping and socio-economic censuses missing or not readily available, and consultations not properly conducted; decisions affecting community livelihoods taken 'on an informal and ad hoc basis without consultation, restoration or compensation'; and works that 'proceeded and triggered demolition in several cases without prior RAPs'. Because of this lack of compliance the Bank suspended all activity on new sub-projects in June 2012 until a plan to put things right was in place. The corrective measures were five retroactive resettlement action plans, one of them for Badia, and six retroactive environmental and social management plans. The report puts the total number of project-affected people under those plans at 2,605 tenants and 319 landlords, and says all the retroactive plans were implemented successfully by the end of the project. On the two Badia demolitions the report says the 2012 one was for the construction of a canal and a road, with affected people in the right of way, and that the February 2013 one was not an activity the project financed, but that the Bank asked Lagos State to apply the project's resettlement policy framework to it. The report also records that Lagos State began paying the compensation under that plan in mid-February 2014.
additions.whole_additions: The project was meant to benefit more than 1.6 million people living in nine slums, which the completion report names as Agege, Ajegunle, Amukoko, Badia, Iwaya, Makoko, Ilaje, Bariga and Ijeshatedo Atire. The report says the Bank's team thought silt and waste could have been removed from the drainage channels by barge in the monsoon season, or from access points about every 100 metres in the dry season, which would have needed almost no resettlement, but that the state was not interested in exploring that. It says the right of way was 15 metres on both sides of the drains, which would have triggered massive resettlement, and that a 5-metre access road along one side only would have been easier for resettlement than the access roads on both sides that Lagos State asked for. On results, the report carries a box of selected impacts taken from 'Lagos is Working', a 2013 document of the project's own coordination unit. That box says that after roads, drains and canals were built, some communities in Agege, Amukoko, Badia, Bariga, Itire, Ilaje, Iwaya and Makoko no longer experience flooding, and that where water used to cost 50 Naira for 25 litres residents were paying around 5 Naira. Those are the project unit's own figures, not a Bank finding.

dropped.reason: Fails tests 1 and 3: no Bank money was ever disbursed, and the Bank's agreements were terminated before the credit became effective. The Note on Cancelled Operation, cover-dated 15 August 2013 with an NCO date of 16 August 2013, was downloaded and read in full from disk, 517 lines of extracted text. Its data sheet gives credit IDA-48650, an original commitment of XDR 779.30 million, a revised amount of XDR 0.00 million and a disbursed amount of XDR 0.00 million, and its disbursement table shows FY12 actual disbursement of 0.00 against 144.20 planned. Its key dates give approval 24 February 2011, planned effectiveness 31 July 2012, original closing 31 August 2016 and actual closing 29 June 2012: the credit was terminated about a month before it was due to become effective. The note's narrative says the Bank investigated corruption allegations and gave evidence to the government, specified in April 2012 conditions that had to be met for the financing to continue, told the government on 29 June 2012 that in the absence of those conditions it had decided to terminate the legal agreements with immediate effect, and that the government informed the Bank on 31 January 2013 that it was withdrawing its request for World Bank financing. The Independent Evaluation Group's ICR Review of 24 March 2014 says 'the project was not implemented' and rates the project non-evaluable on that ground. It records that the proposed project 'potentially affected 76,211 people in 13,526 households, involving the relocation of 20,972 people in 3,886 households' at an estimated cost of US$273.2 million - all appraisal figures, which is the kind of paperwork ICIJ's 73,329 rests on. The Review does say that by the first implementation support mission in July 2011 the social programmes were 'making progress in the payment of compensation funds' and that resettlement sites were being developed, but neither document records any Bank disbursement, advance or retroactive financing against that work; the disbursed amount is zero. Any case on the Padma resettlement would need a different financier, and that is separate research.

dropped.candidate: India Second Kerala State Transport Project (P130339)
dropped.reason: Bucket (c): no harm established. The Bank's Implementation Completion and Results Report of 21 June 2022 (2,515 lines of extracted text, read from disk and searched in full for resettlement, compensation, land acquisition and affected-person terms) gives no count of project-affected people at all, and says at paragraph 54 that 'the project paid appropriate compensation to all PAPs/project affected families (PAFs), except PAFs that opted for a Court ruling to enhance compensation'. It rates social safeguards performance at the end of the project Highly Satisfactory and environmental safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's ICR Review of 1 November 2022 repeats this: delays in land acquisition early on 'were resolved' and the project 'appropriately compensated all Project Affected Persons'. The only land-related loss recorded is to the project itself - a 41 km stretch was dropped because of the time land acquisition would take after India's 2013 land acquisition act came in. ICIJ's figure of 103,480, the highest in this batch, therefore rests on appraisal-stage paperwork with nothing in the completion record to say a resettlement of that size happened. The report records two work-site accidents in 2017, each of which killed one person: the toppling of a church flagpole mast after a nearby retaining wall was excavated, and a water tanker accident. It says both were followed up and compensation was paid to the families. Those two deaths are the only harm the record attributes to the project, with no names, no community and no displacement finding attached, so no card is written here; the owner may wish to see that there are two recorded deaths on this project. Nothing in the Bank's record and no press report, court case or NGO field research on this project's resettlement was found.

dropped.candidate: India National Highways Interconnectivity Improvement Project (P121185)
dropped.reason: Dropped after check. The Bank's completion report of 29 June 2022 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it were read from disk in full. The documents record 775 acres taken, 558 of them private, 6,390 structures affected and 11,138 project-affected people across eleven road corridors in five states, and the only failure either document records is an unquantified delay: the completion report says 'compensation and eligible assistance were duly paid to all PAPs in six of the 11 road corridors' with the other five, in Bihar and West Bengal, transferred to the Green National Highway Corridors Project for their pending resettlement actions to be monitored, and the Independent Evaluation Group says 'disbursement of compensation to project-affected people (PAPs) were substantially delayed in several sections but by project closing, all 11,138 PAPs were compensated for land acquisition for the subprojects completed under the project'. The draft card's whole content was that those two sentences contradict each other. They do not: the Independent Evaluation Group's sentence is limited to 'the subprojects completed under the project', which is the same set as the completion report's six corridors, so no conflict can be printed. What is left is a delay with no number of people, no date, no place and no named community, across a five-state corridor project, with no court record, press report or NGO field research found. That is below the bar for a card.
